Lessons.Title: Other Conditions for Triangle Similarity
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Prove optional SSS and SAS triangle similarity theorems by first dilating one triangle and then applying the corresponding triangle congruence theorem.

This lesson is explicitly optional beyond the core AA requirement. For SSS similarity, if DE/AB=EF/BC=DF/AC=k>0, dilate ABC by k. Its image has three side lengths equal to DEF, so SSS congruence plus a rigid alignment maps the image to DEF. For SAS similarity, matching ratios of two corresponding sides and equality of the angle between them yield the same result via SAS congruence.

The included angle condition matters: if two pairs of proportional side lengths meet at vertices but their given angle is elsewhere, similarity is not automatically established. Theorems require matching side and angle correspondence, positive nondegenerate lengths and a genuine triangle.

Verbal diagram: ABC has sides 4,6,8, DEF corresponding sides 6,9,12. Every quotient is 3/2, so DEF is a uniform dilation (plus possible rigid motion) of ABC. A scalene triangle may be reflected without changing side proportions or similarity.

Student task: prove both optional criteria in writing, then annotate why an SSA-like set of side ratios and a nonincluded angle fails as a general theorem. Teacher rubric (0–4): one consistent k, correct SSS or included SAS hypotheses, full dilation-then-rigid proof, and a valid non-example. Proof and modelling are human scored.

KeyConcepts.Title: SSS similarity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Three pairs of corresponding sides in one common positive ratio guarantee triangle similarity.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Dilate by that ratio and use SSS congruence.

KeyConcepts.Title: SAS similarity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two pairs of proportional corresponding sides and an equal included angle guarantee triangle similarity.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Dilate to match two sides, then use SAS congruence.
KeyConcepts.Example: Adjacent source sides 4,6 and target 8,12, with equal included angle, give k=2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Optional theorem boundary
KeyConcepts.Definition: The similarity shortcuts extend but do not erase the needed angle/side hypotheses of valid congruence criteria.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not assume SSA is sufficient because two side ratios happen to agree.
KeyConcepts.Example: An ambiguous SSA construction may produce two non-similar triangles.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove SSS similarity
WorkedExamples.Question: ABC has corresponding sides 4,6,8; DEF has 6,9,12. Prove similarity.
Steps: Dilate ABC by k=3/2 about any chosen centre.
SSS makes the dilated image congruent to DEF under the given correspondence.
Therefore the original triangles are similar.
WorkedExamples.Check: 4+6>8 and 6+9>12 ensure nondegenerate triangle side sets.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove SAS similarity
WorkedExamples.Question: AB=4,AC=6, ∠BAC=50°; DE=8,DF=12, ∠EDF=50°. Why similar?
WorkedExamples.Method: Scale to match both side lengths and use the included angle.
Steps: Dilate ABC by k=2 so its sides from A have lengths 8 and 12.
Dilations preserve the included angle, keeping it at 50°.
The scaled image matches DE,DF and their included angle; SAS gives congruence to DEF.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Similar at scale 2 by SAS similarity.
WorkedExamples.Check: The 50° angle is between the two listed sides in each triangle.

WorkedExamples.Title: Invalid proportional-side conclusion
WorkedExamples.Question: Two triangles have one known corresponding angle 45° and one pair of sides in ratio 2. Does that force similarity?
WorkedExamples.Method: Check whether enough corresponding facts are known.
Steps: One angle equality gives only one angular constraint.
One side ratio determines a possible scale but says nothing about other sides.
Other angle values may vary, yielding non-similar triangles.
Need AA or valid SSS/SAS similarity data.
WorkedExamples.Check: A counterexample uses 45–45–90 and 45–60–75 triangles, sharing one 45° but differing other angles.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using two corresponding side ratios without knowing the included angle.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The shape may vary with included angle.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Require the included angle for SAS similarity or all three side ratios for SSS.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating SSS similarity as SSS congruence without accounting for scale.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Proportional sides can have differing actual lengths.
CommonMistakes.Correction: First apply the positive dilation so all three target lengths match, then use SSS congruence.

SummaryPoints: SSS and SAS similarity theorems follow from dilation plus the corresponding congruence criteria.
Included angle and ordered side ratios are essential.
Optional deeper proofs and counterexamples require teacher scoring.

Lessons.Title: Splitting Triangle Sides with Dilation, Part 2
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Prove the converse of the proportional-division theorem: a segment parallel to a triangle side divides the other two sides in the same ratio, and apply the equivalence correctly.

Let triangle ABC be nondegenerate, M lie on segment AB, N on segment AC, and MN∥BC. Then ∠AMN=∠ABC and ∠ANM=∠ACB as corresponding angles with parallel lines; the angle at A is common. AA similarity yields AM/AB=AN/AC=MN/BC. The ratios use matching corresponding sides in the SAME direction.

Conversely, for points M on ray AB,N on ray AC satisfying AM/AB=AN/AC=k>0, centre-A dilation maps B→M and C→N, so MN∥BC. The two implications together give equivalence under the described nondegenerate positive-ray conditions.

Verbal diagram: in triangle ABC, line segment MN spans sides AB and AC near vertex A and is parallel to base BC. The small triangle AMN is similar to ABC and its sides are proportional to the matching large triangle sides.

Student task: annotate a triangle with a parallel mid-segment or off-midpoint segment, write a complete AA proof and a separate dilation proof for the converse. Teacher rubric (0–4): precise parallel and ray hypotheses, matching angle pairs, consistent proportional equations, and both logical directions. Actual construction and explanation are teacher assessed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallel-to-proportional theorem
KeyConcepts.Definition: A segment between two sides of a triangle parallel to the third side divides the two sides in a common fraction from their vertex.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use AA similarity of the smaller and original triangle.
KeyConcepts.Example: If MN∥BC and AM/AB=2/5 then AN/AC=2/5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Proportional-to-parallel converse
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal positive fractions along rays AB and AC give a connecting segment parallel to BC.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use the unique centre-A dilation with that factor.

KeyConcepts.Title: Ratio ordering
KeyConcepts.Definition: Corresponding lengths must be compared consistently between the smaller and larger triangle.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use AM/AB=AN/AC=MN/BC, not crossed or inverted pairs.
KeyConcepts.Example: Small-to-large factor 2/3 means all three small/large side ratios are 2/3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove proportionality from a parallel
WorkedExamples.Question: M is on AB, N on AC and MN∥BC. Prove AM/AB=AN/AC.
Steps: Two matching angles give triangle AMN∼ABC by AA.
Their corresponding side ratios match, so AM/AB=AN/AC=MN/BC.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The parallel line splits both sides in the same proportion.
WorkedExamples.Check: A nondegenerate triangle and MN with positive length are assumed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find an unknown cut length
WorkedExamples.Question: AB=15, AM=6, AC=20, MN∥BC. Find AN.
WorkedExamples.Check: Since 0<2/5<1, N lies between A and C as required.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove a segment parallel from ratios
WorkedExamples.Question: AB=12, AM=9, AC=16, AN=12 with M,N on the rays from A. Prove MN∥BC.
WorkedExamples.Method: Check equal scale factors and identify dilation.
Steps: A dilation centred at A with k=3/4 maps B→M and C→N.
The dilation maps line BC (not through A) to line MN parallel to it.
WorkedExamples.Check: This uses the converse, not the forward theorem, and the common ray direction is essential.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using an angle equality without having parallel lines or a valid triangle correspondence.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify exactly which transversal and parallel lines create each equal angle.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating proportions written in inconsistent directions as interchangeable.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It can invert or scramble the scale factor.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write all numerators from the same small triangle and denominators from the large triangle.

SummaryPoints: Parallel-to-side implies a smaller AA-similar triangle and proportional sides.
Equal positive side fractions from a vertex imply parallel segment by dilation.
Both logical directions are distinct claims needing proof and explicit hypotheses.

Lessons.Title: Practice With Proportional Relationships
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Solve exact missing lengths and scale factors in contextual similarity problems, track measurement units, and check the reasonableness of numerical models.

This lesson is optional source practice. A scale drawing with 1 plan unit corresponding to a real-world length u has actual length Lactual=u·Lplan; ratios between corresponding plan and actual lengths remain consistent for every pair. For areas, a length scale k gives an area scale k², not k.

Verbal diagram: a triangular garden is represented by a 3–4–5 right triangle in plan units, each equal to 2.5 feet. The actual side lengths are 7.5,10,12.5 ft, retaining the same right-angle shape. A second garden at twice the dimensions has four times the area.

Original activity: design a rectangular or triangular garden or quilt plan from measurements and a declared scale. Compute two missing lengths, an area scale and explain which quantities are linear versus squared. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct source data and units, consistent ratios, valid answer checks, and model interpretation. Original drawings and partner discussion require human scoring.

KeyConcepts.Title: Proportional length relationship
KeyConcepts.Definition: All corresponding linear measurements share one scale factor k.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Solve Limage=k·Loriginal with consistent units and correspondence.
KeyConcepts.Example: At 1 plan unit=2.5 ft, 4 units represents 10 ft.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area under similarity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Dilation by positive factor k multiplies area by k².
KeyConcepts.Rule: Apply the square of the linear scale, not k, when comparing surface areas.
KeyConcepts.Example: Doubling all side lengths quadruples area.

KeyConcepts.Title: Dimensional analysis
KeyConcepts.Definition: Numerical operations must preserve or convert the physical unit attached to each measurement.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use length units for side lengths, square units for areas, and label ratios explicitly.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 3-by-4 foot rectangle has area 12 ft², not 12 ft.

WorkedExamples.Title: Scale a triangular garden
WorkedExamples.Question: A garden plan has right-triangle sides 3,4,5 units, each unit representing 2.5 ft. Find actual side lengths.
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply each plan side by one conversion factor.
Steps: Scale factor is 2.5 ft per plan unit.
Triangle remains right-angled by uniform scaling.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Actual sides are 7.5 ft, 10 ft and 12.5 ft.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find area change in a scaled quilt
WorkedExamples.Question: An original square patch has area 9 in²; every edge is tripled for a new quilt. Find new area.
WorkedExamples.Check: A 3-inch square becomes a 9-inch square, area 81 in².

WorkedExamples.Title: Solve unknown similar side
WorkedExamples.Question: Two similar triangles have matching sides 6→15 and 8→x. Find x.
WorkedExamples.Method: Set a consistent corresponding length ratio.
Steps: Scale factor from first to second is 15/6=2.5.
WorkedExamples.Answer: x=20 in the same side-length units.
WorkedExamples.Check: The side correspondence and scale direction are fixed throughout.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Scaling area by the linear scale instead of its square.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Both independent dimensions change, so area changes by k·k=k².
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use k² for area and k³ for volume when appropriate.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mixing plan units, feet and square feet in one expression without conversion.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Inconsistent units make the numerical result uninterpretable or wrong.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write a conversion factor with units and label lengths versus areas.

SummaryPoints: Similar figures use one length scale factor for every corresponding side.
Area scales by the factor squared; answer units matter.
Optional source contexts with original designs and written checks are human assessed.
